title: Organizing your library
description: Use tags, tag groups, performers, studios, groups, and saved views to make a growing Cove library easier to revisit.

blocks.text: Cove is built for libraries that become more structured over time. You do not need to classify everything perfectly at the beginning. Add enough structure to make the library easier to find, review, browse, and share each time you return.

blocks.alt: Blank Create Tag form with classification and relationship fields
blocks.caption: A tag can start as a simple reusable name. Add a group, aliases, parent tags, timing thresholds, or custom fields only when they improve how you browse and search.

blocks.text: Start with the record that owns the content, then add only the relationships that improve retrieval:

items: performers and studios for identities reused across items
tags for overlapping classification
tag groups for dividing a larger tag vocabulary into understandable categories
groups for a collection with its own identity or order
saved filters for a view you want to revisit
dynamic groups when a collection should resolve from a query
Scan or import media into Cove.
Add the broad metadata that will help you find it later.
Create views you return to often with saved filters or dynamic groups.
Add more specific structure only where it pays off.
Review provenance when an automated workflow changes something important.

blocks.text: A useful library is not only organized. It is understandable: you can tell what a value means, where it came from, and why an item appears in a collection.

items: the label applies to many otherwise unrelated items
you want the label to be searchable and reusable
you want several overlapping labels on the same item
you are intentionally curating a collection
order or membership matters
the collection should behave like a chosen set instead of a shared label
the collection should update itself
membership comes from a rule, filter, or activity pattern

blocks.text: Some tags describe a whole item. Others describe where a performer, face, tag, or another entity appears inside a video.

items: use normal tags when the whole item should carry the label
use occurrence tagging when timing matters and you need to know where something appears
occurrence tagging works with segments, which also power player bars, filters, and compilations

blocks.text: A growing library usually benefits most from deeper structure in a few places:

items: high-value tags you search often
performer identity cleanup
studio normalization
recurring watch or review queues
groups you revisit often

blocks.text: Once those are stable, add advanced workflows such as contextual tagging, segments, sub-videos, and compilations where they provide a clear benefit.
